items.title: Section: Desire's Category — Eight Similes, and the King Who Was Never Satisfied

items.zh: 謂正尋思：如是諸欲，皆墮黑品。猶如骨鎖，如凝血肉，如草炬火，如一分炭火，如大毒蛇，如夢所見，如假借得諸莊嚴具，如樹端果。
items.en: One rightly investigates: these desires all fall within the dark category. They are like a dry bone; like a lump of raw flesh; like a torch of grass on fire; like a single glowing ember; like a great venomous serpent; like what is seen in a dream; like ornaments borrowed for an occasion; like fruit hanging at a treetop's very end.

items.zh: 追求諸欲諸有情類，於諸欲中，受追求所作苦，受防護所作苦，受親愛失壞所作苦，受無厭足所作苦，受不自在所作苦，受惡行所作苦。如是一切如前應知。如世尊說：習近諸欲有五過患。謂彼諸欲，極少滋味，多諸苦惱、多諸過患。又彼諸欲，於習近時，能令無厭、能令無足、能令無滿。又彼諸欲，常為諸佛及佛弟子，賢善正行、正至善士，以無量門呵責毀呰。又彼諸欲，於習近時，能令諸結積集增長。又彼諸欲，於習近時，我說無有惡不善業而不作者。如是諸欲，令無厭足，多所共有，是非法行、惡行之因。增長欲愛，智者所離，速趣消滅，依託眾緣，是諸放逸危亡之地。無常虛偽妄失之法，猶如幻化，誑惑愚夫。若現法欲、若後法欲、若天上欲、若人中欲，一切皆是魔之所行、魔之所住。於是處所能生無量依意所起惡不善法。所謂貪、瞋及憤諍等。於聖弟子正修學時，能為障礙。由如是等差別因緣，如是諸欲，多分墮在黑品所攝，是名尋思諸欲麁品。云何尋思諸欲麁時？謂正尋思：如是諸欲，去來今世，於常常時、於恒恒時，多諸過患、多諸損惱、多諸疫癘、多諸災害。是名尋思諸欲麁時。云何尋思諸欲麁理？謂正尋思：如是諸欲，由大資糧、由大追求、由大劬勞，及由種種無量差別工巧業處，方能招集生起增長。又彼諸欲，雖善生起、雖善增長，一切多為外攝受事。謂父母、妻子、奴婢、作使、親友、眷屬。或為對治自內有色麁重四大，糜飯長養，常須覆蔽、沐浴、按摩；壞斷、離散、消滅法身，隨所生起種種苦惱。食能對治諸飢渴苦；衣能對治諸寒熱苦，及能覆蔽可慚羞處；臥具能治諸勞睡苦，及能對治經行住苦；病緣醫藥能治病苦。

items.title: Section: Desire's Principle — the Groom Who Priced His Bride Down to Nothing

items.zh: 是故諸欲，唯能對治隨所生起種種苦惱，不應染著而受用之。唯應正念，譬如重病所逼切人，為除病故，服雜穢藥。
items.en: Therefore, these desires are only able to counteract whatever suffering happens to arise — one should not indulge them with attachment. One should only, with right mindfulness, regard them as a person afflicted by grave illness regards taking a foul, bitter medicine solely to be rid of that illness.

items.zh: 又彼諸欲，有至教量，證有麁相。又彼諸欲，如是如是所有麁相，我亦於內現智見轉。又彼諸欲，有比度量，知有麁相。又彼諸欲，從無始來本性麁穢，成就法性、難思法性，不應思議、不應分別，是名尋思諸欲麁理。如是名為由六種事，覺了欲界諸欲麁相。

items.title: Section: The First Dhyāna's Peaceful Mark — Learning the Mark Closes

items.zh: 復能覺了初靜慮中所有靜相。謂欲界中一切麁性，於初靜慮皆無所有。由離欲界諸麁性故，初靜慮中說有靜性。是名覺了初靜慮中所有靜相。
items.en: One is further able to recognise the peaceful mark present within the first dhyāna. That is, every coarse quality found in the desire realm is entirely absent in the first dhyāna; because it is free of every one of the desire realm's coarse qualities, the first dhyāna is said to possess a peaceful nature. This is called recognising the peaceful mark present within the first dhyāna.

items.zh: 即由如是定地作意，於欲界中了為麁相，於初靜慮了為靜相，是故名為了相作意。即此作意，當言猶為聞思間雜。

items.title: Section: Confident Understanding — Moving Beyond Words Into Direct Practice

items.zh: 彼既如是如理尋思，了知諸欲是其麁相，知初靜慮是其靜相。從此已後，超過聞思，唯用修行，於所緣相發起勝解，修奢摩他、毘鉢舍那。既修習已，如所尋思麁相、靜相，數起勝解。如是名為勝解作意。
items.en: Having thus investigated soundly, and having come to know that desire is coarse and the first dhyāna is peaceful, from this point on one moves beyond hearing and reflection, relying solely on cultivation itself — generating vivid understanding with respect to the object, cultivating calm-abiding and insight. Having thus cultivated, one repeatedly generates vivid understanding of the coarse and peaceful marks just as investigated — this is called confident understanding.

blocks.text: The rest of the examination of desire, then the peace of the first absorption. A long passage (0465c27) is untranslated.

Desires "fall within the dark category. They are like a dry bone; a lump of raw flesh; a torch of grass; a glowing ember; a great venomous serpent; what is seen in a dream; ornaments borrowed for an occasion; fruit at a treetop's end." Venerable Miào Jìng on the meat: in the Āgamas, a bird with a piece of meat is chased by many birds. On the single ember: many embers can cook rice; a single one only burns your hand.

Those who pursue desires suffer the pains of seeking, guarding, losing what they love, never being satisfied, lacking freedom, and wrongdoing. The Buddha named five faults of indulging desire: little flavour and much suffering; it brings no satisfaction; it is condemned by all the Buddhas and the good; it increases the fetters; and there is no wrong one will not do for it. Desires of this life and the next, of heaven and of earth, "are all Māra's domain". **Time**: in past, present, and future, always full of danger. **Principle**: desires are gathered only with great effort, and largely serve others (family, servants); or they merely counteract the body's needs: food for hunger, clothes for cold and modesty, bedding for fatigue, medicine for illness.
"These desires can only counteract whatever suffering arises; one should not indulge them with attachment", but regard them "as a person gravely ill regards a foul, bitter medicine".
"Every coarse quality found in the desire realm is entirely absent in the first absorption"; hence it is peaceful.

"From this point on one moves beyond hearing and reflection, relying solely on cultivation": generating vivid understanding of the coarse and the peaceful. Venerable Miào Jìng: not yet form-realm concentration, but cultivation all the same.

quiz.q: Desires are "like a dry bone." What does Master Cháng Bǎi say?
options: chasing desire is like a dog chasing a dry bone — worthless
quiz.why: "They are like a dry bone; like a lump of raw flesh; like a torch of grass on fire; like a single glowing ember." Master Cháng Bǎi: the dry bone likens desires — rebuking beings who chase desire like a dog chasing a dry bone: worthless.

quiz.q: "Like a lump of raw flesh" — what does Venerable Miào Jìng cite from the Āgamas?
options: one bird carries a piece of meat, and all the others fight for it
quiz.why: "Like a lump of raw flesh." Venerable Miào Jìng: the Āgamas explain in detail — chased by many birds: one bird carries a piece of meat, and all the other birds come to fight over it.

quiz.q: "Like a single glowing ember" — how do the masters' readings differ?
options: Miào Jìng: a single ember accomplishes nothing — not enough to cook; Cháng Bǎi: even a little desire destroys all merit
quiz.why: "Like a single glowing ember." Venerable Miào Jìng: many embers together can cook rice and vegetables, but a single ember accomplishes nothing. Master Cháng Bǎi: even a tiny bit of desire destroys all one's merit. The two readings point in opposite directions.

quiz.q: "Like fruit at a treetop's end" — where does Venerable Miào Jìng locate the danger?
options: reaching for it, one may fall and die — approaching desire is like that
quiz.why: "Like ornaments borrowed for an occasion; like fruit hanging at a treetop's very end." Venerable Miào Jìng: wanting to pick that fruit is dangerous — you may fall from the tree and die; approach desire and you face such problems.

quiz.q: "Like one gravely ill taking foul medicine to be cured." How does Master Cháng Bǎi apply this?
options: use sense objects without relish — like medicine for hunger's illness
quiz.why: "One should only, with right mindfulness, regard them as a person afflicted by grave illness regards taking a foul, bitter medicine solely to be rid of that illness." Master Cháng Bǎi: when using these, don't cling to their tastiness — only because of the illness of hunger and thirst, treat them as medicine for one's suffering.

quiz.q: "Every coarseness of the desire realm is absent in the first dhyāna." Why, according to Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: free of the desire realm's distress — no desire, so no desire's suffering
quiz.why: "Every coarse quality found in the desire realm is entirely absent in the first dhyāna." Venerable Miào Jìng: he has left the desire realm's distressing objects and has no desire; the form realm's first dhyāna has no desire, so none of desire's distress.

quiz.q: Confident understanding "moves beyond hearing and reflection." What do the masters say about before and after?
options: Miào Jìng: after a period of study one graduates and studies no more; Cháng Bǎi: at the mark stage, if one forgets the method, one returns to study
quiz.why: "From this point on one moves beyond hearing and reflection, relying solely on cultivation itself — generating vivid understanding with respect to the object." Venerable Miào Jìng: one studies for a time and eventually graduates; after that, beyond hearing and reflection, no more study. Master Cháng Bǎi: at the earlier stage, if in sitting one forgets how to practise six-thing insight, one must return to study or look at notes.
